estimates.method:
Method A, pixel silhouette slices. Scripts and results are in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user/6435a7db-fe21-5f3b-bca9-e49ba2609387/scratchpad/mass/. The pipeline runs seg.py, regions.py, volume.py, compute.py, run_all.py, final.py, report.py, then write_json.py, which writes results_methodA.json.

(1) Mask. I fitted a smooth model of the grey wall and floor (iterated push-pull inpainting). A pixel counts as foreground when its RGB distance from the model is over 22, or its chroma (R-B) is more than 7 above the model, or it is more than 18 darker. Only holes under 150 px are filled, so real gaps such as arm-to-torso windows stay background. A hand-drawn divider polyline separates Ollie from Rex where they touch: the arms at x≈590-625, y≈255-440, and the boot toe against the claw at x≈615. Floor contact shadows are cut off by tight foot polygons. Check images: overlay_regions.png, unassigned.png (only floor shadows are left unassigned) and ov_raw.png.

(2) Regions. Hand polygons from 2-4x zoom grids split each figure into head+neck, crest/horns/ears, torso, upper arm/forearm/hand per side, legs (crotch to pants hem), feet (hem to sole) and tail. Ollie's tail is split into core and tuft. Rex's thigh pouches are cut out of the hip widths.

(3) Volume. Each 1-px slice is an ellipse with area = pi/4 x k x w^2 per run, where k = depth along the camera axis divided by visible width. Upright parts (head, torso) are sliced by image rows. Limbs are first rotated so their axis is vertical; the angles are set by hand because PCA failed on fat blobs. They are Rex arms -6/-16/0 and +16/+8/0 deg, Rex legs -3/+13; Ollie arms -45/+60/0 and +16/-35/0, legs -22/+6. The curved tail, crest, horns and ears use local thickness: sum over pixels of pi/4 x k x t, where t is the diameter of the largest inscribed disc. Synthetic tests: the rotated slicer is exact on a 40-degree cylinder, where plain rows overestimate by 25%. Local thickness is within 1.4% on that cylinder and 18% high on a sphere.

(4) Hidden and modelled parts. Feet use a wedge, V = fill x L x W x H. Rex's hidden tail base is a frustum and Ollie's hidden tail stub is a small cylinder. Rex's tail also gets a foreshortening factor.

(5) Scale. Rex's 3.048 m is set over 790 px, so m/px = 0.0038582, and Ollie uses the same scale as ruled.

(6) Range. The low/high values combine independent log factors in quadrature: depth ratios + fullness (one factor, fully correlated across the body), arm-view asymmetry, feet model, tail extras, mask edge ±1 px (Ollie -2 px for fur), pixel scale ±0.8%, Ollie's perspective, and density. Bounds with every factor at its extreme are also reported.

rex.densitySource: Whole-body density = tissue density diluted by gas in the lungs and gut. Tissue: 1.0812 +/- 0.0099 g/mL in 12 competitive male bodybuilders (8.5% fat), measured by underwater weighing corrected for residual lung volume (Fry, Cisar & Housh 1987, J. Applied Sport Science Research 1(4):61-65). Gas at relaxed mid-breath: about 3.3 L functional residual capacity + half a tidal breath + about 0.1 L gut gas, roughly 0.045 L/kg. These are approximate typical adult-male values; the GLI-2021 equations (Hall et al. 2021, ERJ 57:2000289) give exact predictions. That gives 1/(1/1.0812 + 0.045) = 1.031 g/mL. Low 980 = tissue -1 SD with lungs near total lung capacity (~0.088 L/kg). High 1065 = tissue +1 SD with lungs at residual volume (~0.023 L/kg). Cross-check: young men measure 1.066-1.073 g/mL with residual air removed (Tesch et al. 2022, J Funct Morphol Kinesiol 7:70, already cited in the project), and muscle is about 1,060. Caveat: if Rex has reptile-sized lungs, his density could be about 950-1,000.

estimates.assumptions:
HEIGHT AND SCALE
- Floor row under each body. A standing figure's head is over its ankles, so I used the floor under the ankles, not the toe tips.
- Rex: the left foot sits further back, heel bottom about row 788-790; the right foot points at the camera, toe pads 816, claws 822. His pants hems are at rows 722 and 735, so the right ankle is about 13 px nearer the camera. That puts the floor at about 791 under the left ankle and 804 under the right; mean 798 ± 6.
- Ollie: boot heel/toe rows are 806/815 and 801/813, giving ankle floors of about 809 and 805; mean 807 ± 5.
- Head tops are the visual half-coverage edge. The mask has a 1-2 px antialias halo, so the mask top rows are 6 for Rex and 9 for Ollie.
  - Rex crest tip: row 8 ± 2.
  - Rex skull dome under the spikes: row 40 ± 4.
  - Ollie horn tip: row 11.
  - Ollie hair top: row 24.
  - Ollie skull: about row 34, allowing about 4 cm of hair.
- Rex: 798 - 8 = 790 px, so 3.048 m / 790 px = 0.0038582 m/px. Error is ±0.8% linear and ±2.4% in volume.
- Rex to the skull: 758 px = 2.925 m.
- Ollie at the same scale (as ruled):
  - horn tip: 796 px = 3.071 m
  - hair top: 783 px = 3.021 m
  - skull: 773 px = 2.982 m
- These include about 7 cm of lug sole, so Ollie barefoot to the horn tip is about 3.00 m.
- Perspective: Ollie's floor sits 9 px lower than Rex's, so he is likely about 2% nearer the camera. His true size would then be about 2% smaller (horn height about 3.01 m) and his volume about 6% smaller. This is included as a one-sided low factor of 0.94.
- Camera tilt and keystone are ignored (about 1-2%).

DEPTH RATIOS (k = depth / visible width), and why
I computed the human anchors from the ANSUR II public male CSV (n = 4,082, downloaded from the Penn State OpenLab site; saved as ansur_ratios.json). Values are for all men, then the heaviest 10%, then the 10% with the most V-shaped chest-to-waist ratio:
- chest depth / chest breadth: 0.877, 0.946, 0.842
- waist depth / waist breadth: 0.727, 0.769, 0.698
- buttock depth / hip breadth: 0.710, 0.754, 0.681
- head length / head breadth: 1.294
- foot length / foot breadth: 2.67
- Fullness: ANSUR girths are larger than ellipses with the same breadth and depth (waist 1.054x, buttock 1.090x; chest 1.24x, because the caliper breadth misses the lats). Real trunk sections are boxier than ellipses, so I applied ×1.07 (range 1.00-1.12) to the torso. Without it, an ellipse-only model of the ANSUR mean man comes out about 6% light.

Ratios used:
- Torso chest zone: 0.90 (0.78-1.05). Abdomen: 0.75 for Rex, 0.72 for Ollie (lean visible abs), range 0.62-0.88. Pelvis: 0.72 (0.65-0.85). These bodies are far more muscular than humans: lats widen the outline (which lowers k), while pecs, traps and spinal muscles add depth (which raises it). With no side view I kept near-human values and wide ranges.
- Rex head+neck: 1.05 (0.85-1.30). The head is turned three-quarters and tipped up, so the snout is partly in the silhouette, and the neck is roughly round.
- Ollie's head: 1.25 (1.05-1.45), from ANSUR's 1.29; neck 1.0.
- Upper arms: 1.0 (0.85-1.15); bodybuilder arms are close to round.
- Forearms: 0.9 (0.75-1.05).
- Rex's open clawed hands: 0.6 (0.45-0.8). Ollie's fists: 0.75 (0.6-0.9).
- Thigh, knee and calf in pants: 1.0 (0.85-1.15). Pants count as tight per the brief, though they look a little baggy, which pushes toward the low end.
- Rex's tail: 0.8 (0.6-1.0). The picture shows the tail's side (dorsal spikes on top), so its visible width is its height, and reptile tails are flattened side to side. Foreshortening ×1.12 (1.0-1.25): the tail rests on the floor at about row 757 versus 798 under Rex, so it runs roughly 0.6-1.3 m back from the camera (depending on the unknown lens).
- Rex's hidden tail base: 0.09 m^3 (0.04-0.18).
- Rex's crest spikes: 0.5 (flattened plates). Ollie's horns: 1.0. Ears: 0.25.
- Ollie's tail tuft is hair: packing 0.15 (0.05-0.30).
- Rex's thigh pouches overhang the hips by about 25/20 px. Left in, they would inflate the pelvis ellipse by about 30%. I removed them from the widths and added them back as 0.15 m slabs (0.009 m^3).

ARMS
The two arms of each figure look very different in the picture:
- Rex: image-left arm 0.115 m^3, image-right arm 0.278 (posed broadside).
- Ollie: image-left arm 0.216 m^3 (fully shown), image-right arm 0.048 (turned away and behind the vest).

Treating both bodies as symmetric:
- Central: each arm is the mean of the two views.
- Low: the geometric mean. This is exact if two elliptical limbs are seen from orthogonal sides.
- High: the larger view.

FEET (no side view)
Feet use a wedge: V = fill × L × W × H.
- Rex:
  - W = 0.656 m (170 px across the forward-pointing foot, including splayed toes; range 155-180 px).
  - L/W = 1.2 (0.95-1.6). The turned-out left foot spans only 198 px, so the feet are broad and short; the human ratio of 2.67 does not apply.
  - H = 0.293 m; fill 0.45 (0.35-0.55).
- Ollie's boots:
  - L = 0.70 m (0.58-0.82) and W = 0.30 m (0.25-0.35). These are inferred from boots turned out about 30-45 degrees with visible spans of 152 and 183 px and shafts about 0.4 m wide.
  - H = 0.32 m; fill 0.50 (0.40-0.60).
- Sole outline area = c × L × W, with c = 0.70 (0.60-0.80) for gaps between toes and the boot arch gap.
  - Rex: 0.36 m^2 (0.20-0.62) per foot.
  - Ollie: 0.147 m^2 (0.087-0.23) per boot. On hard floor, lugs alone contact less.

FRONTAL AREA
This is the mask pixel count × scale², with real gaps excluded.
- Rex: 4.92 m^2, of which the tail is 0.47 m^2.
- Ollie: 4.48 m^2, including the hair tuft.

DENSITY
1,030 kg/m^3 (980-1,065). The derivation is in densitySource.

RANGE
Volume uncertainty factors (low / high multipliers on the central volume):

| Factor | Rex | Ollie |
|---|---|---|
| Depth ratios + fullness | 0.842 / 1.184 | 0.835 / 1.201 |
| Arm view | 0.985 / 1.071 | 0.974 / 1.071 |
| Feet | 0.971 / 1.049 | 0.987 / 1.018 |
| Tail extras | 0.973 / 1.045 | 0.997 / 1.004 |
| Mask edge | 0.971 / 1.030 | 0.947 / 1.027 |
| Scale | 0.976 / 1.024 | 0.976 / 1.024 |
| Perspective | — | 0.94 / 1.0 |

- These are combined in quadrature with density (0.951 / 1.034).
- With every factor at its extreme at once, the bounds are 1,670-3,580 kg for Rex and 1,610-3,480 kg for Ollie.
estimates.sanity:
HUMAN REFERENCES SCALED TO 3.048 m (mass × (3.048/h)^3)
- Average man, 75 kg at 1.75 m: 396 kg.
- ANSUR II mean man, 85.5 kg at 1.756 m: 447 kg.
- ANSUR II heaviest 10%, 113 kg at 1.815 m: 535 kg.
- Large bodybuilder, 125-136 kg at 1.78 m: 630-680 kg. At 150 kg and 1.80 m: 730 kg.

HOW THE ESTIMATES COMPARE
- Rex at 2,360 kg (1,950-2,880) is about 6x the scaled average man and about 3.5-3.8x a scaled top bodybuilder.
- Ollie at 2,430 kg (1,970-2,970) is similar.

WHY THE PICTURE SUPPORTS THAT
- Arm-to-arm width is about 2.15 m for both figures. A scaled ANSUR man's shoulder width is 0.89 m, so they are 2.4x wider.
- Rex's torso alone is 0.94 m wide on average and 1.20 m at most. A scaled human's is about 0.5-0.6 m.
- Ollie's crotch is at 0.335 of his height, against 0.47 for humans. His torso region is therefore about 1.4x longer relative to height and about 2.2x wider, which is why his torso is 66% of his volume.
- Simple isotropic-thickening check: scaled ANSUR man × (width ratio)^2 gives 447 × 2.43^2 ≈ 2,630 kg for Rex and 457 × 2.39^2 ≈ 2,610 kg for Ollie. Both agree with the slice results to within about 10%.

SEGMENT SHARES
- Rex: torso 47%, arms 17%, legs 17%, tail 9%, feet 6%, head 4%.
- A human's trunk is about 50% of mass. Rex's extra share sits in the tail and the huge feet.

METHOD AND MASK CHECKS
- Synthetic tests pass: the rotated slicer is exact on a tilted cylinder; local thickness is within 1.4% on a tube and 18% high on a sphere.
- Region overlays were checked by eye (overlay_regions.png). Only floor shadows are left unassigned (unassigned.png).

CAVEATS
- Depth is the dominant unknown, worth about ±15-20%.
- Treating the pants and Ollie's fur outline as body pushes toward the high side.

NOTE ON THE SHARED FOLDER
A separate Method B run has written its own files into the same folder: results.json, results_method_b.json, method_b.py, mask.npy and others. I did not write, check or overwrite those files; my results are in results_methodA.json. Its Rex volume, 2.34 m^3, is within 2.5% of this method's 2.29 m^3. It also uses a 800 px height scale and a 1,060 density.

estimates.method:
METHOD B, segment solids. The scripts and outputs are in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user/6435a7db-fe21-5f3b-bca9-e49ba2609387/scratchpad/mass/method_b/: method_b.py (main), segdefs.py (every hand-read pixel measurement), geom.py, seg3.py (silhouette), overlay_segments.png (segment polygons, axes and stations drawn on the picture), results.json (summary) and results_method_b.json (full detail). The mass/ folder is shared with another agent working in parallel, so all of my files are in the method_b/ subfolder. I briefly moved that agent's seg.py and bg.npy into my folder by mistake and then put them back unchanged. None of its scripts read my files.

(1) Silhouette. The grey studio background was modelled by iterative normalized convolution (Gaussian sigma 25 px, wall and floor fitted separately). Foreground is colour distance > 20 or local std > 9; on the floor, pixels > 45 levels darker than the floor model. Holes were filled only if < 600 px or dark (clothing). The two figures were separated by a hand-drawn polyline along the edge of Ollie's arm, fist and boot, because Ollie's arm overlaps Rex's forearm.

(2) Heights were read on 4-6x gridded zooms. The ground line is the mean of the two foot-contact centres, because the feet sit at different depths. Rex's far foot touches at about y 798 and his near foot at about y 819, so his ground is 808.5. The tip of his tallest crest spike is at y 8.5, giving 800.0 px = 3.048 m, so the scale is 0.003810 m/px. The same scale is used for Ollie: ground 812, horn tip y 12.5.

(3) Trunk. Left and right silhouette edges were read by hand at 15 stations (y 128-543 for Rex, y 108-558 for Ollie). They exclude the arms, the flat cargo-pocket flaps and the vest buckle straps. The trunk was integrated in 1-px slices with an elliptic cross-section, area = pi/4*w*(k*w), where k varies with height (chest, then waist, then pelvis, then crotch).

(4) Arms. Each arm part (upper arm, forearm, hand) has a hand-drawn polygon and axis. Chord widths perpendicular to the axis were measured every 1 px from the silhouette and stacked as elliptic sections. The slices sweep 94-99% of the polygon area. For Ollie, 3 px of fur fringe was removed from each width.

(5) Legs. Thigh (crotch to knee) and shank (knee to cuff) widths were read every 10-20 px for each leg separately and stacked with circular-ish sections.

(6) Head is an ellipsoid; neck a cylinder; crest, horns and ears are small solids; hands are silhouette area x thickness; Ollie's fists are ellipsoids; feet and boots are breadth x assumed length x height x fill.

(7) Rex's tail was measured along its curve. Nine stations from where it emerges behind his near leg to the tip. Perpendicular thickness = vertical chord x cos(local slope). Arcs and thicknesses were scaled up for perspective. The hidden root section is modelled as an elliptic frustum. All tail pieces are elliptic frustums.

(8) Uncertainty. Every assumed ratio has a central value and a 90% interval. A 40,000-draw Monte Carlo correlates the nine depth ratios (rho = 0.85, one shared 'how deep did the artist imagine him' factor) and adds: 3% width-reading error per body group, 0.6% overall scale error from ground-line ambiguity, 5% model-form error, and density drawn from a triangular distribution. Low and high are the 5th and 95th percentiles of mass; the volume range comes from the same run. Deterministic all-low and all-high extremes are also given below.

rex.densitySource: Two-compartment body model: fat 900 kg/m^3, fat-free mass 1,100 kg/m^3 (Siri 1961; Brozek et al. 1963, Ann NY Acad Sci 110:113). Siri's equation, density = 495/(%fat + 450), gives 1,071-1,081 for an 8-12% fat, very muscular body; elite male bodybuilders measure about 5-10% fat by densitometry (e.g. Withers et al. 1997, Aust J Sci Med Sport). Skeletal muscle is about 1,060 (Mendez & Keys 1960, Metabolism 9:184: 1.0597 g/cm^3; Ward & Lieber 2005, J Biomech 38:2317, report 1.055-1.112 for fixed human muscle). Hydrostatic body density has residual lung volume and about 100 mL of gut gas subtracted. A living body also carries lung air: an adult male's resting lung volume (FRC) is about 3 L, roughly 3.5-4% of an 80 L body, which puts a lean human at about 1,035-1,045 whole-body. For these hyper-muscular giants, lungs plausibly scale with the skeleton (height cubed) rather than with muscle: scaled FRC is about 16 L, under 1% of 2.3 m^3. Central 1,060 assumes about 1.5% total gas: 1,076/1.015. Low 1,010 = human-proportioned lungs at mid-breath plus about 15% fat. High 1,085 = about 5% fat and minimal gas. Not assumed: bird-like air sacs, which would put Rex nearer 900-1,000 (dinosaur volumetric studies usually use about 1,000 including air spaces, e.g. Hutchinson et al. 2011, PLoS ONE); he is drawn as a mammal-like humanoid.

FRONT VIEW HIDES DEPTH. Every cross-section is an ellipse of area pi/4*w*(k*w), with w the measured frontal width. Values are central [90% interval].

- CHEST k = 0.66 [0.58-0.80]. ANSUR chest depth/breadth is 0.877, but its caliper chest breadth (289 mm) is narrower than the frontal silhouette, because chest circumference (1,059 mm) includes the lats. An ellipse with the measured depth and circumference gives depth / equivalent breadth = 0.618 (SD 0.04), and 0.622 for heavy, lean-waisted men. Raised a little and skewed high because both characters are drawn with hugely protruding pecs and thick backs, and their arms hide part of the lats.
- WAIST k = 0.80 [0.70-0.88]. ANSUR waist depth/breadth 0.727 (0.712 for muscular-ish men). The waist circumference implies a fuller-than-ellipse section (superellipse n about 2.7, area factor 0.864 vs 0.785), so area-equivalent k is about 0.79-0.81.
- PELVIS k = 0.84 [0.74-0.92] at buttock level (top third of belt-to-crotch). ANSUR buttock depth/hip breadth 0.71, with circumference-based area factor giving 0.84-0.87. It falls linearly to CROTCH k = 0.66 [0.58-0.76], because two touching thighs give 0.5-0.69 (ANSUR thigh circumference 625 mm against a hip silhouette of about 340 mm gives about 0.66).
- THIGH k = 1.00 [0.88-1.12]: thighs are near-circular (circumference 625 mm, about 199 mm diameter).

- NECK k = 1.0 [0.85-1.10].
- HEADS: Rex length/breadth 1.40 [1.2-1.6] (ANSUR head length/breadth 1.29, plus a snout); his breadth was back-solved from the three-quarter view. Ollie 1.32 [1.2-1.45]; his face height was divided by cos 25 deg for the backward head tilt.

Symmetry: each figure's arm that is partly hidden (Rex's right, behind Ollie's arm; Ollie's left, behind his own turned torso) is replaced by a mirror of the fully visible arm. Using the arms as visible instead cuts the central mass by about 6% (Rex 2,330 kg, Ollie 2,260 kg); the frontal areas add the hidden arm area back.

Perspective: the camera height was estimated from the curvature of belts and pant cuffs. Rex's belt sags about 8-10 px over a 120 px half-width and the cuffs about 10 px over 60 px, which puts the horizon near y 200-300 and the camera about 8-11 m away, i.e. a telephoto (about 20 deg vertical field of view). estimates.method:
METHOD C, anthropometric segment scaling. All files are in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user/6435a7db-fe21-5f3b-bca9-e49ba2609387/scratchpad/mass/method_c/: method_c.py (model and Monte Carlo), area.py, write_results.py, annotate.py, crop.py; results in method_c_results.json and method_c_raw.json; every pixel reading is drawn on method_c_measurements.png; zoomed grid crops are c_*.png. Nothing under /home/user/dino-strength-sim was touched. I reused two things from the shared folder: the figure masks ../rex_fig.npy and ../ol_fig.npy (checked on ov_masks.png and used only for silhouette area and run widths), and the ANSUR II male public CSV in ../ansur_dl/male.csv (OPEN Design Lab, Penn State, n=4,082).

(1) Scale. Rex's crest tip is at row 8.5, found by a row-by-row colour-difference scan. His ground (ankle-plane) row is 800.5 ±8: claw tips touch at 800 and 820, pads at about 795 and 812. That gives 792 px = 3.048 m, so 0.0038485 m/px. Ollie uses the same scale. His ground row is 807.5 (boot toes at 815–818). Horn tip is at 13.5, hair top at 24.5, skull top at about 34.5.

(2) Human reference. The reference is the ANSUR II mean man: 1.7562 m, 85.52 kg. Segment volumes are de Leva (1996) male mass fractions divided by Dempster segment densities (Winter, Table 4.1). This gives tissue 81.1 L, which matches the Siri tissue volume at about 20% fat (81.2 L). I added FRC 3.3 L (Quanjer 1993 ERS) and 0.1 L of gut gas to the trunk, for a living envelope of 84.5 L (implied density 1,012, a check that it is realistic). The trunk is split into upper/middle/lower parts using de Leva's sub-segments, with boundaries at C7/suprasternale, xiphoid, navel and hip joint. Reference lengths are ANSUR landmark heights or de Leva joint-centre lengths. Reference widths are ANSUR breadths for the torso (chest 289, waist 326, hip 346 mm) and circumference/π for the limbs (flexed biceps, flexed forearm, wrist, thigh, lower thigh, calf, ankle), plus head breadth and length and foot breadth.

(3) Segment formula. Each segment volume = V_human × (L_fig/L_hum) × (W_fig/W_hum) × depth ratio, in metres. Depth ratio = (H_fig/H_hum) × [(W_fig/H_fig)/(W_hum/H_hum)]^k, where H is the skull-top height (comparable to ANSUR stature). k = 1 is the squared-width rule. Exceptions:
- Rex's upper arms and forearms: his two arms are seen from different sides (105 px and 165 px at the biceps belly), so their product is used as width × depth and no k is needed.
- Heads: head length is set explicitly (Rex's head is turned about 40°; Ollie has a muzzle).
- Feet: foot length is assumed.
- Middle trunk uses the RMS of chest and waist widths; lower trunk uses the RMS of waist and hip widths, on both the figure and the human.

(4) Tail. Rex's tail is a chain of elliptical frusta (a tapered cone):
- Hidden part: from the rump to where it emerges beside his right calf. It is 0.95 m long, tapering from 155 px (0.60 m) to 105 px (0.40 m) tall.
- Visible part: profile measured perpendicular to the tail axis at 105, 94, 79, 57, 45, 35 and 22 px, then 0, over 305 px (1.17 m).
- Width/height ratio is 0.8.

Ollie's tail is a fleshy cone plus the hair switch.

(5) Uncertainty. A 40,000-sample Monte Carlo, using triangular distributions, draws every landmark row and width (in px), the ground row, the skull top, a perspective/proportion factor (0.97–1.03), Ollie's relative distance (0.97–1.03), the depth exponents (trunk k 0.7–1.0–1.2; limbs 0.85–1.0–1.1, shared within a figure), the foot and tail assumptions, a model-form factor for how well human shape factors fit these bodies (0.88–1.12), and density. Reported low/high are the 2.5–97.5 percentiles; the central value has every input at its mode. Frontal area = mask pixels × s², with floor shadows clipped below each foot. The ANSUR and bodybuilder proportion table is in method_c_results.json.

DEPTH. A front view cannot show depth, so every segment's depth is tied to its width through the exponent k.
- k = 1 (central) keeps the ANSUR II mean man's cross-section shape. ANSUR depth/breadth ratios: chest 0.877, waist 0.727, buttock depth to hip breadth 0.710; limbs treated as round (circumference/pi).
- Evidence from ANSUR II (n=4,082 men; computed in this run): across men, torso depth grows at least as fast as breadth (log-log slope of depth on breadth: OLS 0.92 chest, 1.20 waist, 1.25 hip; reduced major axis 1.4-1.7). The 5% with the largest flexed-biceps/stature have deeper sections (chest 0.956 vs 0.877; waist 0.76 vs 0.73; hip 0.75 vs 0.71). So k = 1 is not generous.
- The range still allows a flatter V-taper cartoon torso (lats add breadth without depth): trunk k is 0.7/1.0/1.2. Limbs are drawn as round muscle balls and baggy columns: limb k is 0.85/1.0/1.1. Each figure uses one shared trunk k and one shared limb k, so the error is not averaged away.
- Depth alone moves the volume by -12%/+10% for Rex and -18%/+14% for Ollie.
- Rex's arms are seen at different angles (105 vs 165 px at the biceps, 129 vs 150 px on the forearm), so their product is used as width x depth (+/-20%).
